{"sample_id": "blind-17b68f03d8824363837223860cc05f65", "theorem": "Consider a prime $p$ of the form $4 t+3$. Show that $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$ iff $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "number_theory", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), which is odd.

Suppose first that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\), so \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Since \((a^m)^2\equiv1\pmod p\), we have \(a^m\equiv\pm1\pmod p\). It cannot be \(1\), since then the order of \(a\) would divide \(m<2m\). Hence \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Because \(m\) is odd,
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
If \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \(a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\). Thus \(2m\mid2n\), so \(m\mid n\). Consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\). Then
\[
a^m=(-1)^m(-a)^m\equiv-1\pmod p,
\]
and \(a^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(a^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \((-a)^{2n}=a^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid2n\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(m\mid n\); write \(n=qm\). Now
\[
1\equiv a^n=(a^m)^q\equiv(-1)^q\pmod p.
\]
As \(p\) is odd, this forces \(q\) to be even. Hence \(2m\mid n\). Since also \(a^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p\), it follows that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=2m=p-1\). Therefore \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\)."}
